paragraphs: A high speed nose is not styling, it is pressure management. The long tapered front exists to soften the shock wave a train produces entering a tunnel, and its exact shape is the result of wind tunnel work rather than of a designer's pen. Get that profile wrong and the train reads as a toy however good the rest is.

The mesh runs 707,277 polygons and 747,659 vertices in quads and tris with mixed UV layout. This build is simplified, which refers to the interior rather than the shell, and that is the correct saving on a train almost always seen from outside.

This page is unusually deep, with seven other builds from $119 to $179, including versions with interiors, on railway, and rigged. Aimed at rail marketing and infrastructure visualisation, travel advertising, news graphics, simulators and games. Built to CheckMate specification, on sale since 2026.

A cruiser is defined by its stance: a low seat, forward controls, a wide rear tyre and a V-twin left visible between the frame tubes rather than hidden behind panels. The Scout carries that arrangement with a cast frame that uses the engine as a stressed member, which is why the machine looks so compact around the middle.

The mesh runs 288,010 polygons and 291,863 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 57 texture maps - 8 at 4096x4096 and 49 at 2048x2048. Fifty-seven maps on a motorcycle is a lot, and it goes into the chrome, the castings and the badge work.

A rigged build sits on this page at $129. The static model at $119 covers motorcycle advertising and dealership visualisation, lifestyle and travel imagery, film and television, and games. On sale since 2017.

A flying saucer alone is a prop; a saucer with its occupants is a scene. This collection supplies both, and the figures arrive rigged, which is what allows a landing, an emergence and a gesture rather than a static tableau under a hovering disc.

Buying craft and characters together also keeps the scale honest between them, which is exactly the thing that goes wrong when a vehicle and its crew come from different sources and the doorway turns out to be the wrong size.

At $119 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits science fiction film and television, games, advertising and comedy content, motion graphics, book and poster illustration, and themed events. On sale since 2021.

A locomotive with a wagon behind it is a working train rather than a museum exhibit. That pairing changes what the asset can do: it can be shown pulling, shunting or standing in a yard, and the consist can be extended by repeating the wagon rather than needing a second purchase.

The mesh runs 517,572 polygons and 549,332 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 34 texture maps - 20 at 4096x4096 and 14 at 2048x2048, carrying the soot, the rust and the painted lettering that steam era stock always wears.
At $119 it suits period film and television, rail heritage and museum work, industrial era scenes, model railway and simulator projects, and games. On sale since 2015.

A short passenger set is what most regional railways actually run: a power car and two coaches, one first class and one second, with different seating densities and window spacing between them. That distinction between the classes is a detail worth having, because it is visible from outside and it dates and locates the train.

The mesh is large at 1,665,792 polygons and 1,669,884 vertices with mixed UV layout, spread across three vehicles built to the same standard rather than a detailed leading car pulling simplified ones.
At $119 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits regional rail and transport visualisation, station and infrastructure scenes, travel advertising, simulators and games. On sale since 2026.

An Ohio class boat is defined by the long flat run of deck behind the sail, which is where the missile tubes sit. That section gives the submarine its enormous length and its distinctive profile, quite different from an attack boat where the hull tapers away much sooner behind the fin.

The mesh is efficient at 208,584 polygons and 222,345 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 6 texture maps all at 8192x8192. A submarine hull is largely smooth, so the texture carries the plating seams, the flood ports and the anechoic tiling.

This page carries an animated build at $149 and a rigged version at $139. The static model at $119 covers naval and defence visualisation, documentary and news graphics, strategic analysis material, and games. On sale since 2017.

An attack submarine is shorter and finer than a missile boat, with the hull tapering back from the sail toward a single propulsor. The Virginia class replaced the traditional periscope with photonics masts, which is why the sail carries no through-hull optics and looks cleaner than earlier designs.

The mesh is deliberately economical at 66,113 polygons and 67,193 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 11 texture maps including 4 at 8192x8192. That split is the right one for a smooth hull: the geometry is simple, and the surface detail is entirely texture.
A rigged build sits on this page at $139. The static model at $119 covers naval and defence visualisation, documentary and news graphics, strategic analysis material, and games. On sale since 2017.

A four-engine starfighter with splitting wings is one of the most familiar shapes in science fiction, and the split is the whole mechanism: the wings open into an X for combat and close for cruise, moving the engines and the wingtip cannons with them. A static model can only ever show one of those two states.

This build arrives rigged, which is what makes the mechanism usable: the wings can be opened, closed or animated between the two, and the landing gear posed. The mesh runs 288,807 polygons and 318,972 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs.
At $119 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits science fiction film and television, games, fan and hobby projects, previsualisation, motion graphics and illustration. On sale since 2024.

An aircraft tug is built around one number: the mass it has to move. That gives it a very low profile so it fits under a nose, enormous ballast for traction, four wheel drive and steering, and a cab offset or lowered so the driver can see the nose gear. Nothing about it looks like an ordinary vehicle.

The mesh runs 820,471 polygons and 834,462 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 23 texture maps at 4096x4096 carrying the high visibility paint, the ballast castings and the apron grime.

A rigged build sits on this page at $129. The static model at $99 covers airport and ground handling visualisation, aviation services marketing, apron scenes, training material and games. On sale since 2017.

A proximity suit is mirror-finished for a reason: the aluminised outer layer reflects radiant heat rather than absorbing it, which is what lets a wearer work close to burning fuel. That reflectivity is also the hardest thing to render convincingly, because the suit picks up its whole environment across every fold.

The mesh is light at 14,430 polygons and 14,621 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 6 texture maps at 4096x4096 carrying the fabric weave, the visor and the seams that break the reflection.

At $99 it suits firefighting and industrial safety visualisation, aviation rescue and refinery scenes, safety training material, film and television, and games. On sale since 2017, kept to real-world scale so it fits a standard figure.

The alert configuration is the one worth modelling: launcher erected, canisters raised toward the sky, stabilisers deployed and the vehicle set up rather than travelling. That is the state a defence graphic almost always needs, and it is visually completely different from the same system on the move.
The mesh runs 650,026 polygons and 348,255 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the density in the canister frame, the hydraulics and the chassis running gear.

At $99 and built to StemCell specification, it suits air defence and military visualisation, news and documentary graphics, training material and games. Real-world scale is kept, so it sits correctly beside other vehicles in a battery. On sale since 2024.

Mechanic's overalls are a single garment from collar to ankle with no waistband to break the line, which changes how the fabric gathers at the hips and the knees. The chest pockets, the front zip and the elasticated back are the details that make it read as workwear rather than as a jumpsuit.

The mesh is minimal at 3,445 polygons and 3,532 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 7 texture maps at a mix of sizes up to 4096x4096. That economy suits a garment usually needed on several figures in a workshop scene.

At $99 it suits automotive workshop and service visualisation, garage and dealership scenes, vocational education and recruitment material, character set dressing and games. On sale since 2020, kept to real-world scale so it fits a standard figure.

Household cavalry ceremonial dress is one of the most elaborate uniforms still worn anywhere: a polished cuirass over a scarlet tunic, a plumed helmet, white breeches and thigh-length boots. Every element is regulated to the inch, and it is a uniform people photograph constantly, which leaves no room for approximation.
The mesh runs 48,218 polygons and 49,611 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 15 texture maps at 4096x4096 carrying the polished metal, the wool nap and the gold lace.

At $99 it suits ceremonial and state occasion visualisation, tourism and heritage material, film and television costume, museum presentation and games. On sale since 2017, kept to real-world scale so it fits a standard figure.

A cargo scanner is a portal rather than a machine: a shielded tunnel large enough for a pallet or a vehicle, with a conveyor through it, an operator cabin alongside and warning barriers around the approach. The scale is the point, and it is what distinguishes cargo screening from the baggage scanners at a passenger checkpoint.
The mesh runs 227,649 polygons and 259,034 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the density in the tunnel structure, the conveyor and the control equipment.

At $99 and built to StemCell specification, it suits border control and customs visualisation, port and logistics presentation, security industry marketing, airport cargo scenes, training material and games. On sale since 2021.
